Installing and running¶

Priroda has no installer. You copy an executable, the basis-set files you need and, for parallel runs, the MPI launcher into a directory, write an input file, and start the program with the input and output file names as arguments.

Executables¶

Linux¶

The official site lists these Linux files. Sizes and dates are those of the 2025 file index.

File

Date

Description

p

2023-06-25

Main x86-64 executable, statically linked.

p4

2023-06-25

Build “for FMA/AVX2” processors.

p_d

2021-11-12

Dynamically linked build.

p4_d

2025-02-28

Dynamically linked FMA/AVX2 build.

p_l

2025-04-14

Build for a particular cluster, started through the site’s Intel MPI wrapper.

p_mvs1p1, p_mvs10p, p_mvs10q

2019–2023

Builds for particular clusters.

p_arm, mpiexec_arm

2015-09-23

ARM build and its MPI launcher.

mpiexec

2012-09-09

MPI launcher shipped with p.

xm

2025-04-24

The developer’s molecule viewer. It takes a Priroda input file as its argument (xm C60.qm.in).

That p is statically linked is inferred from the description of p_d as “dynamically linked”. The site does not say which cluster each p_mvs* and p_l build is for.

Older distributions used other names: p6, p6_32 and p6_64 for version 6, p9, and p1 for version 11 at one site. Scripts and forum posts written for those versions use these names. This manual writes p throughout.

Some users run the Linux build under WSL on Windows.

Windows¶

The Windows build is a Cygwin build for x86-64. It is in the exe64/ directory of the official site:

File

Date

Description

p1.exe

2021-10-01

Serial executable.

p1_190306.exe

2019-03-12

Older serial build.

p_190306.exe

2019-03-12

Older parallel (MPI) build.

xm.exe

2019-03-08

Viewer.

cygwin1.dll

2021-10-01

Cygwin runtime library.

For serial runs you need only p1.exe and cygwin1.dll in the same directory. A full Cygwin installation is not required, and no administrator rights are needed. For parallel runs see Parallel runs on Windows.

Note

In 2017 users referred to the parallel Windows build as exe64/p.exe. The current index has no p.exe; the newest parallel build there is p_190306.exe.

Old 32-bit Windows builds could not allocate more than about 1 GB of memory; malloc(...) failed appeared above that. Users report that the 64-bit build has no such limit.

Running a calculation¶

Serial runs¶

Give the input file first and the output file second:

p input.in output.out

On Windows:

p1.exe input.in output.out

On Linux the current directory is usually not in PATH, so start the program as ./p or with its full path. If the program cannot find the input or the basis file, give full paths everywhere: for the executable, the input, the output, and the basis file inside the input.

Run in a directory you own and can write to. Keep file and directory names to Latin letters, digits and simple punctuation, with no spaces or Cyrillic. This also applies to the computer name on Windows. File names are case-sensitive on Linux, although keywords are not.

Note

One user saw the complaint 0: output file 'tasK.out'? when the output file name contained a capital letter. This is not confirmed. Lower-case file names avoid the question.

Older versions also wrote the output to standard output when no output file was given.

Parallel runs on Linux¶

Priroda is parallelized with MPI. Three command forms appear in the sources, and which one works depends on the build:

p -np 4 input.in output.out                  # the executable starts its own processes
./mpiexec -np 4 ./p input.in output.out      # the mpiexec shipped with p
mpiexec -np 4 p input.in                     # as used for version 14 at one site

The first form is what users ran with versions 6 and 10. The second is what the official site shows for the current p and its bundled mpiexec. In one report with version 10, starting through the bundled mpiexec failed while p -np 4 worked, but that run also had a relative basis-file path, which can cause the same failure. Try the form from the official site first.

Check the start of the output. A parallel run prints the number of processes and one line per process:

 parallel on  4 processors
 node  0: 'linux-ldmm'
 node  1: 'linux-ldmm'
 ...

The cluster builds are started through the cluster’s own MPI. The official example for p_l under SLURM is:

sbatch -p test -n 16 -t 6 impi ~/bin/p_l file.{in,out}

Here impi is that cluster’s wrapper script for Intel MPI, not part of Priroda.

Parallel runs on Windows¶

The official site shows this command for a two-process run:

mpirun.exe -np 2 p.exe C60.qm.in C60.qm.w.2.out

The MPI runtime is not on the site. Users assembled it from Cygwin as follows:

  1. Download the 64-bit Cygwin installer (setup-x86_64.exe from https://cygwin.com). Install the default packages plus the openmpi package.

  2. Copy these files from the Cygwin installation into the directory with the Priroda executable: cygwin1.dll, cyggcc_s-seh-1.dll, cygmpi-12.dll, cygopen-pal-13.dll, cygopen-rte-12.dll, orterun.exe. Newer OpenMPI packages have cygopen-pal-40.dll and cygopen-rte-40.dll instead of the -13/-12 files; take those. Take cygwin1.dll from the same installation, because the other DLLs work only with matching versions. After this, Cygwin itself is no longer needed.

  3. Create a directory dev one level above the directory you start Priroda from, with subdirectories shm and mqueue. For Priroda in C:\Priroda, that means C:\dev\shm and C:\dev\mqueue. Without a Cygwin installation, the Cygwin libraries take the parent of the start directory as the root /.

  4. If the program is in a system directory such as C:\Program Files, run it as administrator.

  5. Set TMPDIR and start the run from cmd.exe:

    cd /d "C:\Priroda"
set TMPDIR="%TEMP%"
orterun.exe -np 2 p.exe "C:\Work\file.in" "C:\Work\file.out"

Problems reported with this setup:

  • The recipe needs a Priroda build that supports parallel runs. Version 6 (p6.exe) failed with an OpenMPI agent-not-found error; users moved to version 17.

  • On a computer connected by Wi-Fi that also has a wired network adapter, OpenMPI stops with tcp_peer_send_blocking: send() to socket 12 failed: Transport endpoint is not connected (128). Disable the wired adapter.

  • With the Ethernet cable unplugged, one user’s run used only two of the cores.

  • Warning: '/dev/shm' does not exists or is not a directory. means the Cygwin environment is missing. Create the dev directories (step 3), or start from a Cygwin shell.

Warning

A user reported in 2021 that this recipe no longer worked on Windows 10 with a current Cygwin, and no fix was posted. Expect to adapt it to the Cygwin and OpenMPI versions you have.

Memory, disk and scratch: $system¶

The $system group sets the resources. Every limit applies per MPI process. disk=10 on four processes can use up to 40 GB.

$system memory=2048 disk=-2048 path=/scratch/user $end
memory

Memory in MB. Two values set rank 0 and the other ranks separately: mem=2048,256 gives the master process 2048 MB and every other process 256 MB. In a parallel run, most of the memory and all of the disk storage are used by rank 0, so give the other ranks less.

disk

A positive value is scratch disk in GB. The program opens one scratch file per gigabyte. A negative value is scratch kept in memory, in MB (a RAM disk): disk=-2048 holds 2048 MB of scratch in RAM. A second value applies to the other ranks, as for memory; the official example inputs typically give them -1.

path

The scratch directory. A colon-separated list gives one directory per process, which pays off only when the directories are on different physical drives. For several processes and one fast disk, a single directory is enough.

Keeping scratch in memory¶

With a negative disk, memory plus |disk| must fit into the physical RAM for each process, or the run stops at once with malloc(...) failed. One user’s setting for a 24 GB node is memory=9000 disk=-14000. Keeping the scratch in RAM is faster than any disk. In one RI-MP2 benchmark on 8 cores it cut the time from 86 minutes (scratch on disk) to 12.4 minutes.

Where scratch files go¶

The scratch directory is taken from path=, then from the TMPDIR environment variable. The files are named tmp<number>.<rank>, for example /tmp/tmp2960.0. Priroda deletes them at the end of a normal run; after a crash, delete the leftovers yourself.

Note

The fallback when neither path= nor TMPDIR is set is reported differently. input.txt says the current working directory. A 2020 user report says the directory of the input file. Version 6 printed Disk: 1 GB '/tmp' when $system was omitted. Set path= or TMPDIR explicitly.

On Windows there is no /tmp. Without path= or TMPDIR, older versions stopped after printing 0: opening file /tmp/tmp2960.0. Use $system path=. $end (the current directory) or set TMPDIR.

Disk speed¶

Warning

Never put scratch files on NFS or another network file system. On most clusters the home directories are on NFS; use the node-local scratch disk instead.

Priroda is sensitive to disk speed. Priroda’s own documentation (input.txt) warns that for all methods except GGA DFT, performance “will be degraded terribly” if more than one process reads and writes large files on the same physical drive. In order of preference:

  1. keep the scratch in RAM (negative disk) if it fits;

  2. give each process its own physical drive with path=a:b:c:d;

  3. put all processes on one fast local disk (SSD), accepting some loss.

If the disk is the bottleneck for RI-MP2 or RI-DFT, $integral direct=1 recomputes the integrals instead of storing them. One user found it uses about a third of the memory but runs about ten times longer in CPU time. In a disk-bound RI-MP2 optimization another user got 20 steps overnight with it instead of 2.

Users also recommend more RAM over faster disks. Scratch on a separate SSD helps, but RAM matters more.

When the limits are too small¶

Priroda does not fall back to a slower algorithm when memory or scratch runs out. The run stops with an error such as malloc(536870912) failed (memory) or 0: out of disk space (VNNNN), 184441541KB (scratch). The number in the disk message is the amount needed. Raise the limit in $system, move to a node with more resources, or choose a cheaper method (RI-MP2 instead of conventional MP2).

If you omit $system, version 6 printed Memory: 128 (128) MB and Disk: 1 GB '/tmp'. Defaults in current versions are not documented, so always give $system for anything larger than a test.

If a run fails for lack of memory or disk, see Memory, disk and scratch errors.

Parallel performance¶

Users consistently report the following:

  • DFT scales well within one node, up to about 6–8 cores. Beyond 8 cores the gain is at most about 10%, even for large systems. One 38-step optimization took 101, 63 and 37 s on single nodes with 8, 12 and 24 cores. A small PBE/L1 optimization with version 10 took 81.5, 42.5, 29.8 and 29.3 s on 1–4 cores.

  • Running across nodes gives no gain for DFT. Use one node per job.

  • Memory per process does not drop when you add processes, and in a parallel Hessian nearly all of the disk use is on rank 0.

  • RI-MP2 parallelizes better than DFT, at least in memory. The v5 documentation limits useful parallelism to Nproc ≤ min(N_atoms, N_occ) and recommends a number of processes that divides the number of occupied orbitals nearly evenly. For N_occ = 14 it rates 2, 7 or 14 processes as best, 3 or 5 as acceptable, 6 as poor and 13 as very bad.

  • Small RI jobs on many processes can hang. RI-MP2 and RI-DFT hang with no message when a process receives no work. The output then shows a line 0 blocks ... on node N after integral estimates. Run small RI jobs on one or a few cores.

  • Several independent jobs often beat one parallel job. On a 4-core machine, four single-core jobs ran about 30% faster in total than the same jobs run one after another on 4 cores each.

Results can differ in the last digits between runs on different numbers of processes. An unstable TS search was once seen to follow different paths for different -np.

Note

Older versions scaled worse. In version 6 a parallel Hessian could use at most 2 cores and could hang on 4, and a version 7 MP2 run hung on more than about 24 cores. Use version 17 or later for parallel work.

Hangs, crashes and poor speed-up in parallel runs are covered in Parallel and MPI problems.

Batch systems¶

Priroda needs nothing special from a batch system. The job script has to:

  1. request one node and the number of cores you will use (see parallel performance above);

  2. point the scratch to the node’s local disk or to RAM, by exporting TMPDIR or by path= in $system;

  3. make the memory request cover memory + |negative disk| for every process;

  4. start Priroda with the input and output file names.

A SLURM script along these lines should work. Directory names and module setup are site-specific.

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=mol
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=8
#SBATCH --time=24:00:00

PRIRODA=$HOME/priroda/p                      # full path to the executable
cd "$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR"
export TMPDIR=/local/scratch/$SLURM_JOB_ID   # node-local disk; site-specific
mkdir -p "$TMPDIR"

"$PRIRODA" -np "$SLURM_NTASKS" mol.in mol.out
# or, if your build needs it:  ./mpiexec -np "$SLURM_NTASKS" "$PRIRODA" mol.in mol.out

rm -rf "$TMPDIR"

Under PBS/Torque the same steps read the number of cores from $PBS_NODEFILE. PBS often provides a per-job local scratch directory and deletes it after the job.

#!/bin/bash
#PBS -N mol
#PBS -l nodes=1:ppn=8,walltime=24:00:00

cd "$PBS_O_WORKDIR"
NP=$(wc -l < "$PBS_NODEFILE")
export TMPDIR=/local/scratch/$PBS_JOBID      # site-specific
mkdir -p "$TMPDIR"

$HOME/priroda/p -np "$NP" mol.in mol.out

rm -rf "$TMPDIR"

If /tmp on the node is small or has a quota, a large job dies writing a scratch file, for example 0: write file /tmp/tmp9633.11 (leAX): .... Point the scratch at the cluster’s scratch file system or at RAM.

Note

Historical: the KNC wrappers. The Kazan Scientific Centre clusters (2006–2012) provided the wrappers pbspriroda5, pbspriroda5-mpi and pbspriroda6, called as pbspriroda6 file_name -time hh:mm:ss -queue queue -mem MB -disk size -procs 1:ppn=N. The wrappers wrote the $system group themselves from -mem and -disk, so inputs submitted through them had to omit $system. Forum posts and old FAQs that mention these commands refer to that site only.

Input file requirements¶

The input is a plain text file. Write it in a plain-text editor, not a word processor.

  • Plain ASCII. Keywords, values and file names should contain ASCII characters only. Do not save the file as Unicode.

  • Unix line endings (LF). This holds on Windows too. Saving from Word as “plain text” still leaves Windows (CRLF) line endings, and some editors need to be told explicitly to write Unix line endings.

  • Straight quotes. Write basis="3z.bas" with the ASCII double quote. Typographic quotes, as in basis=»3z.bas», break the basis-file name.

An input with CRLF line endings fails in $molecule, because the carriage return becomes part of the keyword. The output stops after a line like this, where the keyword z-matrix or cartesian is shown garbled by the carriage return:

 molecule input: ''
' ?matrix

Variants seen are ?rtesian for cartesian, 'z-matrix' ?, and 'cartesian followed by ' ? on the next line. A less obvious case: an input edited in Word ran task=scan as a plain optimization.

To check and fix the line endings on Linux:

file mol.in        # reports "with CRLF line terminators" if the file has Windows endings
dos2unix mol.in

Running dos2unix on a file that already has Unix line endings does no harm. On Windows, Notepad++ and the FAR Manager editor (Shift+F2, then UNIX (LF)) can convert line endings.

For the full list of input-reading failures and their symptoms, see The input is not read, or is read wrongly.

Basis-set files¶

The basis sets, their auxiliary (fitting) sets and the ECPs are read from a separate file named by $control basis. The set itself is chosen with set= in $molecule; without it, the default set of the file is used. Without basis=, the basis data are read from the input file itself.

Give the basis file as a full path:

$control task=optimize basis=/home/user/priroda/basis/basis.in $end

A relative name is looked up relative to the directory the program runs in. One user’s parallel run stopped after the node list with application called MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1) - process 0 and worked once the basis file was given with its full path.

  • Put the name in double quotes if the path contains special characters: basis="/data/basis sets/basis.in". Two single quotes do not work; basis=''3z.bas'' fails with error opening file ''3z.bas''.

  • Windows paths work: basis=D:\NMR\Nature\basis\6-31+G(d).

  • The relativistic file basis4.in needs four=1 in $control. Without it the basis input fails.

Which basis files exist and which sets they contain is described with $control basis.
